rows.verified: Crowd-safety roles and responsibilities must be clearly defined for normal and emergency situations.
Event organisers retain overall responsibility for public safety even when tasks such as stewarding are allocated to contractors.
Organisers should liaise with local authorities, emergency services, police and other organisations involved in crowd management.
Crowd risks must be assessed across arrival, entry, movement within the venue, exit and dispersal.
Risk controls should consider young people and people with disabilities or learning difficulties.
Organisers should assess attendance, audience profile and venue suitability and create a crowd-management plan.
Crowd controls should cover arrival and entry, onsite circulation, and departure and dispersal.
Crowd-management methods should be monitored, reviewed after events and improved following incidents or operational learning.
Crowd controls depend on attendance, audience profile, venue design, entry and exit capacity, transport, weather, behaviour, staffing and emergency coordination.
Crowd evidence is event-, venue-, audience- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level crushing or injury probability.
Electricity can kill or severely injure people and can damage property.
Electrical hazards include shock, burns, arcing, fire, explosion and static ignition of flammable vapours or dusts.
Suitable precautions when working with or near electricity can significantly reduce risks to workers and others.
Electrical equipment must be maintained to prevent danger.
The type and frequency of checks, inspections and testing depend on the equipment, its environment and previous results.
Safe electrical working practices apply to people who work on or near electrical equipment and to managers and supervisors controlling that work.
Where possible, electrical supplies should be isolated and secured so they cannot be re-energised during work.
If the supply cannot be turned off, a competent person should advise on a safe method of work.
Electrical controls depend on voltage, fault energy, system design, earthing, isolation, environment, equipment condition, work method and competence.
Electrical evidence is system-, equipment-, task- and condition-specific and is not an exact parcel-level shock, fire or explosion probability.
